title: Digital Marketing Fundamentals
description: What digital marketing is, who you are selling to, and how a funnel, a persona and a KPI fit together.

lessons.title: What digital marketing actually is
lessons.description: The three jobs every piece of digital marketing does, and why weakness in one breaks the others.
lessons.content:
## Learn

**Digital marketing** is everything a business does to find, win and keep
customers using digital channels: search engines, websites, email, social media,
video, messaging apps, and paid ads on any of them.

That is the whole definition. Notice what it does not say. It does not say
"posting on Instagram". Posting is one activity inside digital marketing, the
way pouring concrete is one activity inside building a house.

Every piece of digital marketing does one of three jobs:

1. **Get found** — a person who has never heard of you ends up looking at
   something of yours.
2. **Get chosen** — that person decides you are worth their money or their email
   address, rather than the alternative.
3. **Get kept** — that person buys again, and tells someone else.

### An analogy

Think of a shop on a high street. Three things decide whether it survives:
whether people walk past it, whether the window makes them come in, and whether
they come back next month.

Digital marketing is the same three things, except the street is a search
results page or a social feed, the window is your website, and coming back is an
email you send. The difference is that online you can *see* each step happening.
You know how many walked past, how many came in, and what the sign cost you.

```
      GET FOUND              GET CHOSEN            GET KEPT
   +---------------+      +---------------+     +---------------+
   | search        |      | website       |     | email         |
   | social feed   | ---> | landing page  | --> | WhatsApp      |
   | video         |      | reviews       |     | retargeting   |
   | paid ads      |      | the offer     |     | loyalty       |
   +---------------+      +---------------+     +---------------+
      a stranger             a visitor            a customer
         |                      |                     |
         +--- you can measure every arrow ------------+
```

The arrows are the point. A business that only works on "get found" collects
visitors who never buy. A business that only works on "get kept" runs out of
people to keep.

## Demo

**Petal & Pine** is a fictional direct-to-consumer skincare brand. They sell one
product line online, with no shops. Here is one customer, start to finish.

**Get found.** Priya types *how to fix dry skin in winter* into a search engine.
Petal & Pine has an article answering exactly that, so it appears in the
results. She clicks. Petal & Pine did not pay for this click; the article earns
it. That is **SEO**, covered in module 3.

**Get chosen.** The article is genuinely useful and does not read like an
advert. At the end it offers a free winter skincare checklist in exchange for an
email address. Priya gives hers. She is now a **lead**: someone who has shown
interest and whom the business can contact.

**Get kept.** Over the next two weeks Priya gets three emails. The first sends
the checklist. The second explains why skin dries out in cold weather. The third
offers a starter set. She buys it. Six weeks later an email asks if she is
running low. She reorders.

Count the channels: search, website, email. No social media at all. Petal & Pine
chose those three because that is where their customers already were. That
choice is the strategy, and it is covered in lesson 9.

## Hands-on practice

Pick a business you actually know — where you buy coffee, your gym, a brand you
follow. Work out how it does the three jobs.

Do not research it. Use only what you have personally seen. The gaps you cannot
fill are the interesting part: they are either things the business does not do,
or things it does badly enough that you never noticed.

:::worksheet Three jobs audit
Business:
What they sell:

GET FOUND
- Where did I first come across them?
- What else might bring a stranger to them?
- Did they pay for that, or earn it?

GET CHOSEN
- What convinced me they were worth it?
- What nearly stopped me?
- What proof did they show me (reviews, photos, a guarantee)?

GET KEPT
- Have they contacted me since?
- Would I buy again? Why, or why not?
- Have I ever recommended them to anyone?

THE GAP
- Which of the three jobs are they weakest at?
- One thing I would change first:
:::

## Common mistakes

**Treating digital marketing as "doing social media".** Social is one channel.
Petal & Pine built a business on search and email without it. Starting from
"which platform should we be on" skips the only question that matters: where are
our customers already looking?

**Starting with the tactic instead of the customer.** "We need a YouTube
channel" is a tactic with no reason attached. "Our customers search for how-to
videos before buying, and we have none" is a reason, and it happens to lead to
the same tactic. Only one of those survives contact with reality.

**Working on one job and ignoring the other two.** The most common version is
pouring everything into getting found, then sending all that traffic to a
website that gives people no reason to act.

**Assuming it is free because there is no media bill.** The article that found
Priya took someone a day to write. That day is a real cost. Digital marketing
shifts the cost from media buying to time and skill; it does not remove it.

**Expecting it to work immediately.** Paid ads can start the same day. Search
and content take months. A plan that needs results next week and relies on SEO
is not a plan.

## Key takeaways

- Digital marketing is finding, winning and keeping customers through digital
  channels — not one platform, and not just posting.
- Every activity does one of three jobs: get found, get chosen, get kept.
- Weakness in any one job breaks the other two.
- The channel is a consequence of where your customers already are, never the
  starting point.
- The real advantage over traditional marketing is that every step can be
  measured, which is what the rest of this course teaches you to do.

lessons.title: Traditional marketing and digital marketing
lessons.description: Targeting, measurement, speed and cost shape - the four differences that actually change the job.
lessons.content:
## Learn

**Traditional marketing** reaches people through channels that are not digital:
television, radio, print, billboards, flyers, events and word of mouth.
**Digital marketing** reaches them through digital ones.

The useful difference is not "old versus new". Plenty of traditional marketing
still works. The differences that change how you do the job are these four.

**Targeting.** A billboard is seen by everyone who passes it. A search ad is
seen by people who typed a specific thing. Traditional marketing buys a
*location*; digital marketing buys an *audience*.

**Measurement.** A newspaper advert tells you how many copies were printed. A
digital campaign tells you who clicked, what they did next, and whether they
bought. You still have to interpret it honestly, which module 11 covers.

**Speed of change.** Reprinting a flyer takes days and money. Changing ad text
takes a minute. This is why digital marketing is built around testing.

**Cost shape.** Traditional marketing usually needs a large payment before
anything happens. Digital usually lets you start small and increase what works.

### An analogy

Traditional marketing is a megaphone in a town square. You shout once, loudly.
Some of the right people hear it, along with everyone else, and you never learn
which.

Digital marketing is a conversation at a counter. You say something, you see the
reaction, you say the next thing differently. Cheaper per person, but it only
works if you actually look at the reaction.

```
  TRADITIONAL                          DIGITAL
  +------------------+                 +------------------+
  | one message      |                 | many versions    |
  | to everyone      |                 | to segments      |
  +--------+---------+                 +--------+---------+
           |                                    |
           v                                    v
  +------------------+                 +------------------+
  | guess the result |                 | measure, then    |
  | from sales       |                 | change it today  |
  +------------------+                 +------------------+

  strong at: reach, trust,             strong at: targeting,
  physical presence, local             measurement, speed,
  awareness at scale                   starting small
```

Neither column is the winner. A dental clinic with a billboard outside the train
station and a search ad for *emergency dentist* is using each for what it is good
at.

## Demo

**Bright Mile Dental** is a fictional single-location dental clinic. They have a
small budget and want new patients. Compare two ways to spend it.

**The traditional option.** Ten thousand leaflets through doors in the
surrounding postcodes. Everyone in those homes sees it once. Most do not need a
dentist that week, and the clinic cannot tell which of the handful of new
patients came from the leaflet unless it asks each one.

**The digital option.** A search ad that appears only when someone nearby
searches *dentist near me* or *emergency dentist*. Far fewer people see it. But
every one of them is actively looking for a dentist right now, and the clinic
can see how many clicked and how many then booked.

**The honest comparison.** The leaflet reaches more people. The search ad
reaches better people. For a clinic that needs bookings this month, the ad wins.
For a new clinic that nobody has heard of, the leaflet builds awareness the ad
cannot, because nobody searches for a name they have never seen.

Bright Mile does both, and uses the leaflet to drive a search: *"Search Bright
Mile Dental"*. Now the leaflet's effect shows up as a rise in people searching
the clinic's name, which is measurable.

## Hands-on practice

Take one local business and plan one traditional and one digital activity for
it, then decide which you would fund first and write down why.

The reasoning matters more than the answer. There is no rule that says digital
wins.

:::worksheet Channel comparison
Business:
What they need (more enquiries / more awareness / more repeat custom):

TRADITIONAL OPTION
- What exactly:
- Who sees it:
- How I would know if it worked:
- Rough effort or cost:

DIGITAL OPTION
- What exactly:
- Who sees it:
- How I would know if it worked:
- Rough effort or cost:

DECISION
- Which I would fund first:
- Why:
- What would have to be true for the other one to be the better choice:
:::

## Common mistakes

**Assuming digital is always cheaper.** Competitive search terms can cost more
per enquiry than a leaflet drop. Cheaper per *person reached* is not the same as
cheaper per *customer won*.

**Assuming traditional is dead.** Radio, print and events still work for some
audiences and some products. A course that tells you otherwise is selling you
something.

**Measuring digital properly and traditional not at all, then concluding digital
works better.** This is the most common mistake in the whole comparison. If you
only count what is easy to count, you will always conclude that the easy-to-count
thing is better. Give the leaflet a trackable prompt before you judge it.

**Treating them as separate.** Bright Mile's leaflet makes the search ad cheaper,
because people searching a brand name convert better than people searching a
category. The channels feed each other.

**Running the same message on both.** A billboard has two seconds and no
targeting. An email has a minute and knows who it is talking to. The same words
cannot be right for both.

## Key takeaways

- The real differences are targeting, measurement, speed of change and cost
  shape — not old versus new.
- Traditional buys a location; digital buys an audience.
- Digital's advantage is that you can see what happened and change it today.
- Traditional still wins at broad local awareness, which is often what makes
  digital work better.
- Judge both by cost per customer won, and make sure you can actually measure
  the traditional one before you compare.

lessons.title: The digital marketing ecosystem
lessons.description: Owned, earned and paid media, the channels inside each, and why everything points at owned.
lessons.content:
## Learn

The **digital marketing ecosystem** is the full set of channels available to
you, and how they connect. Learning it early stops you from thinking the job is
one channel you happen to have heard of.

Channels group into three kinds of media, and the grouping tells you what each
one costs and how much control you have.

**Owned media** is what you control: your website, your landing pages, your
email list, your WhatsApp list. You do not pay per person reached. Nobody can
take it away. It is slow to build.

**Earned media** is attention other people give you: search rankings, press
coverage, reviews, someone recommending you. It is the most trusted and the
least controllable. You cannot buy it directly, only do things that make it
likely.

**Paid media** is attention you rent: search ads, social ads, video ads,
sponsorships. It starts the day you pay and stops the day you stop.

### An analogy

Owned media is a house you are building. Earned media is your reputation in the
neighbourhood. Paid media is a hotel room — instant, comfortable, and gone the
moment you stop paying.

You need all three. A business with only paid media has no asset: the day the
budget stops, so does everything. A business with only owned media has a
beautiful house nobody visits.

```
                      +----------------------+
                      |     PAID MEDIA       |
                      | search ads, social   |
                      | ads, video, display  |
                      | fast, rented, stops  |
                      +----------+-----------+
                                 |
                                 v  sends traffic to
  +--------------------+   +-----+--------------+   +-------------------+
  |   EARNED MEDIA     |-->|    OWNED MEDIA     |<--|   EARNED MEDIA    |
  | search rankings    |   | website, landing   |   | reviews, word of  |
  | press, mentions    |   | pages, email list, |   | mouth, shares     |
  | slow, trusted      |   | WhatsApp list      |   | slow, trusted     |
  +--------------------+   +---------+----------+   +-------------------+
                                     |
                                     v
                           +---------------------+
                           |  CUSTOMER, then     |
                           |  repeat customer    |
                           +---------------------+
```

Everything points at owned media. That is not decoration — it is the single most
useful thing to understand about the ecosystem. Paid and earned media are both
ways of filling something you own.

### The channels themselves

- **Search** — SEO (earned) and search ads (paid). Catches people who are
  already looking. Modules 3, 7 and 16.
- **Content** — articles, guides, videos. Feeds search and social. Module 4.
- **Social media** — organic posting (earned reach) and social ads (paid).
  Modules 5 and 6.
- **Video** — YouTube as both a search engine and a social platform. Module 8.
- **Email** — owned, cheap, and the best-converting channel most businesses
  have. Module 9.
- **Messaging** — WhatsApp and chat. Owned, immediate, easy to overdo. Module 10.
- **Websites and landing pages** — where nearly every other channel sends
  people. Modules 2 and 12.
- **Analytics** — not a channel, the nervous system connecting them. Module 11.

## Demo

**Craftwise Academy** is a fictional business selling online courses. Watch one
piece of work travel across the ecosystem.

They publish a free guide: *How to pick your first online course*. That is
**content**, sitting on their website, so it is **owned**.

It starts ranking for people searching that question. That ranking is **earned**
— they did not pay for the position, the article earned it.

They put a small budget behind the guide on social so more of the right people
see it sooner. That is **paid**.

Readers who want the follow-up worksheet give an email address. The list is
**owned**, and grew because of the paid and earned traffic.

A reader posts the guide in a study group. That share is **earned** and cost
nothing.

Three months later, Craftwise emails the list about a new course. The sale comes
from the **owned** channel — but it exists because of everything upstream.

One guide. All three media types. The email list is the asset that remains after
the ad budget is spent.

## Hands-on practice

Map a business you know onto the ecosystem. The gaps are the point: almost every
small business has strong paid or strong owned, and nothing joining them.

:::worksheet Ecosystem map
Business:

OWNED
- Website or landing page:
- Email list (roughly how big, if you can tell):
- Anything else they control:

EARNED
- Do they rank for anything I would search?
- Reviews — where, and are they good?
- Has anyone I know mentioned them?

PAID
- Have I seen an ad from them? Where?
- What was the ad trying to get me to do?

THE JOINS
- Where does their paid media send people?
- Does that destination ask for an email address or just show products?
- What is the one missing join that would make the rest work harder?
:::

## Common mistakes

**Building only on rented land.** A business whose entire presence is a social
account is one policy change away from losing its audience. Use social to build
an email list, not instead of one.

**Expecting earned media on demand.** You cannot schedule a search ranking or a
recommendation. You can only publish things worth ranking and recommending, then
wait. Budget months, not weeks.

**Sending paid traffic to the home page.** The home page answers "who are you".
An ad has already answered that. Send the click to a page about the exact thing
the ad promised — module 2 covers this.

**Choosing channels by familiarity.** Teams pick the platform they personally
use. Craftwise's customers were searching, not scrolling, which is why search
led.

**Ignoring analytics until the end.** If you cannot see which part of the
ecosystem produced a customer, you will keep funding the loudest channel rather
than the best one.

## Key takeaways

- Channels divide into owned, earned and paid, and the division tells you what
  each costs and how much control you have.
- Paid and earned media exist to fill owned media; owned media is the asset you
  keep.
- A business with no owned media is renting its entire audience.
- Earned media is the most trusted and the slowest, so start it early.
- Analytics is what turns a list of channels into a system you can steer.

lessons.title: The customer journey and the marketing funnel
lessons.description: The six funnel stages, what message each one needs, and why the funnel is a loop.
lessons.content:
## Learn

The **customer journey** is the path a person takes from not knowing you exist
to buying from you, and ideally to buying again. The **marketing funnel** is the
simplified model marketers use to describe that path and plan work against it.

It is drawn as a funnel because the numbers shrink at every step. Many people
hear of you, fewer look properly, fewer still buy. That shrinking is normal, not
a failure.

The standard stages:

- **Awareness** — they learn you exist.
- **Interest** — they want to know more.
- **Consideration** — they are comparing you with alternatives.
- **Conversion** — they buy, book or sign up.
- **Retention** — they stay, and buy again.
- **Advocacy** — they tell someone else.

Each stage needs different marketing. Someone at awareness is not ready for a
discount code; someone at consideration does not need an explainer of the basic
problem. Sending the wrong message to the wrong stage is the most common waste in
digital marketing.

### An analogy

Think of dating rather than selling. You do not propose on the first message.
Awareness is being introduced. Interest is a conversation. Consideration is
meeting the friends. Conversion is the commitment. Retention is the relationship
afterwards.

A business that opens with "BUY NOW, 40% OFF" is proposing to a stranger. It
works occasionally, which is exactly why people keep doing it.

```
  people
  reached
    ####################################   AWARENESS    blog, social, video, ads
     ##############################        INTEREST     guides, newsletters
       #####################               CONSIDERATION comparisons, reviews, demos
          ############                     CONVERSION   landing page, offer, checkout
            ########                       RETENTION    email, support, reorder
              ####                         ADVOCACY     referrals, reviews, shares
```

The funnel is a model, not a law. Real journeys loop: people leave, come back
three months later, read a review, forget, then buy from a retargeting ad. The
funnel is still useful because it tells you *what kind of message* someone needs,
even when the order is messy.

### Why retention sits inside the funnel

Many beginners stop the funnel at conversion. That is why so many businesses
spend everything on new customers and nothing on the ones they already have.
Winning a customer back is usually far easier than finding a new one, because
the hardest step — trust — is already done.

## Demo

**Petal & Pine** maps its funnel. One stage, one job, one measurement.

**Awareness.** An article answering *why does my skin get dry in winter*. Job:
be found by someone who has the problem but does not know the brand. Measured by
visitors from search.

**Interest.** At the end of the article, a free winter skincare checklist for an
email address. Job: turn an anonymous reader into a contactable lead. Measured by
checklist sign-ups.

**Consideration.** An email comparing moisturiser types honestly, including when
you do not need theirs. Job: be the brand that was useful rather than pushy.
Measured by replies and clicks through to product pages.

**Conversion.** A product page with real photographs, the full ingredient list,
and reviews from people with the same skin type. Job: remove the last doubt.
Measured by purchases.

**Retention.** A reorder reminder timed to when the bottle should be running
low, plus a short guide on using it properly. Job: second purchase. Measured by
repeat purchase rate.

**Advocacy.** Two weeks after the second order, an email asking for a review.
Job: produce the proof that makes the consideration stage work for the next
person. Measured by reviews received.

Notice how advocacy feeds back into consideration. The funnel is a loop.

## Hands-on practice

Map your own real journey for something you bought in the last six months and
genuinely thought about. Not an impulse purchase.

You will find stages where you cannot remember what the business did. Those are
usually the stages where it did nothing, and you got there on your own.

:::worksheet Journey map
What I bought:
Roughly how long from first hearing about it to buying:

AWARENESS   How did I first hear of it?
INTEREST    What made me want to know more?
CONSIDERATION  What else did I compare it with? What decided it?
CONVERSION  What finally made me buy? What nearly stopped me?
RETENTION   Have they contacted me since? Was it useful or annoying?
ADVOCACY    Have I recommended it? What would make me?

ANALYSIS
- Which stage did the business handle best?
- Which stage did I get through with no help from them?
- If I ran their marketing, which stage would I fix first, and why?
:::

## Common mistakes

**Selling at the awareness stage.** A person who has just learned you exist is
not ready to buy. Asking immediately usually loses them for good.

**Stopping the funnel at conversion.** Retention and advocacy are where profit
and proof come from. A funnel that ends at the sale throws away both.

**Assuming the journey is tidy and one-directional.** People loop, pause and
restart. Build for return visits — retargeting and email exist for exactly this.

**Measuring only the last click.** The retargeting ad gets the credit, the
article that started everything gets none, so the article gets cut. Module 11
covers attribution and why this is a trap.

**Having no awareness activity at all.** Businesses that only run conversion
campaigns slowly run out of people who have heard of them, then wonder why their
ads got expensive.

## Key takeaways

- The funnel describes what kind of message someone needs, stage by stage.
- The six stages are awareness, interest, consideration, conversion, retention
  and advocacy.
- Numbers shrinking at each stage is normal; the job is to shrink them less.
- Retention and advocacy are part of the funnel, and advocacy feeds the
  consideration stage for the next customer.
- Real journeys loop and pause, so build for people who come back later.

lessons.title: B2B and B2C marketing
lessons.description: Who decides, how long it takes and what counts as proof when you sell to an organisation.
lessons.content:
## Learn

**B2C** means business to consumer: you sell to a person buying for themselves.
**B2B** means business to business: you sell to an organisation.

The channels are mostly the same. What changes is who decides, how long it
takes, and what convinces them.

**Who decides.** In B2C, usually one person, sometimes with a partner's opinion.
In B2B, several people: the person who will use it, the person who pays, and
often someone in security, legal or procurement. Each wants different things,
and any one of them can say no.

**How long it takes.** A B2C skincare purchase might take ten minutes. A B2B
software purchase takes weeks or months, with gaps where nothing happens because
the buyer is busy with their actual job.

**What convinces them.** B2C buying is personal: how it looks, how it feels,
whether people like them use it. B2B buying is defensible: the buyer must be
able to justify the choice to someone else. "It looked nice" does not survive
that conversation; "it cut our processing time and here is the case study" does.

**Order size and relationship.** B2B deals are usually larger and fewer, so
losing one matters. That is why B2B marketing invests in relationships and
B2C invests in reach.

### An analogy

B2C is a market stall. People walk past, something catches their eye, they buy
it and walk on.

B2B is applying for a mortgage. Several people review it, each checking a
different thing, it takes weeks, and everyone involved is more worried about
making a bad decision than a brilliant one.

That last point explains most of B2B marketing. **Your buyer is managing risk.**
Case studies, security documentation, trials and references all exist to reduce
the chance that your buyer looks foolish for choosing you.

```
            B2C                                  B2B
  +---------------------+            +-----------------------------+
  | one buyer           |            | user + budget holder + IT    |
  | minutes to days     |            | weeks to months              |
  | emotional, personal |            | justifiable, documented      |
  | many small orders   |            | few large orders             |
  | wide reach wins     |            | right few accounts win       |
  +---------------------+            +-----------------------------+

  proof that works:                  proof that works:
  reviews, photos, social proof      case studies, numbers, references,
                                     trials, security answers
```

### Where they overlap

Both are people. A B2B buyer still reads on a phone, still ignores jargon, still
decides emotionally and justifies rationally afterwards. B2B marketing that
forgets there is a human reading it produces the grey, lifeless content the
field is known for.

## Demo

Compare two of this course's fictional brands.

**Petal & Pine (B2C).** One buyer, deciding for herself. The journey is short:
an article, a checklist, a few emails, a purchase. What convinces her is
photographs of real results, an ingredient list she can understand, and reviews
from people with her skin type. Marketing works at reach — thousands of people,
small orders, fast decisions.

**Shiftly (B2B).** Fictional shift-scheduling software sold to operations
managers. Three people are involved: the operations manager who feels the pain,
the finance lead who approves the spend, and an IT contact who asks where the
data is stored.

So Shiftly produces three different things. For the operations manager, a guide
on cutting the time spent building rotas. For the finance lead, a short case
study with a before-and-after on overtime costs. For IT, a plain page describing
data handling that can be forwarded without a meeting.

The sales cycle is six weeks with two silent fortnights. Shiftly's email
nurture exists to survive those silences. One customer is worth more than a
hundred Petal & Pine orders, so the effort per lead is far higher.

**The same tactic, used differently.** Both run email. Petal & Pine's is a
sequence of six short messages over two weeks to thousands of people. Shiftly's
is a handful of longer, personalised messages to a few hundred, each one giving
the buyer something they can forward to a colleague.

## Hands-on practice

Take one product and write the marketing for both models. This is the fastest
way to feel the difference.

Use a laptop. Selling it to a student is B2C. Selling two hundred of them to a
company is B2B.

:::worksheet B2C and B2B comparison
Product:

AS B2C
- Who decides:
- How long from first contact to purchase:
- The one thing that convinces them:
- The proof I would show:
- Headline I would write:

AS B2B
- Who is involved in the decision (list all of them):
- What each one is worried about:
- How long the decision takes:
- The one thing that convinces the budget holder:
- The proof I would show:
- Headline I would write:

THE DIFFERENCE
- Which single change between the two versions is the biggest?
- Which model would I rather market, and honestly why?
:::

## Common mistakes

**Marketing to the user and forgetting the budget holder.** The operations
manager loves Shiftly and cannot sign anything. Content that only speaks to the
user stalls at the approval step.

**Using B2C urgency in B2B.** Countdown timers and flash discounts read as
desperate to someone making a considered purchase with other people watching.

**Writing B2B content with no personality because it is "professional".** The
reader is a person having a dull Tuesday. Clear and human beats grey and formal
every time.

**Assuming B2B means LinkedIn only.** B2B buyers search for solutions like
everyone else. Search often outperforms social for B2B precisely because it
catches intent.

**Expecting B2B results on a B2C timeline.** Judging a six-week sales cycle
after three weeks tells you nothing, and is how good campaigns get cancelled.

## Key takeaways

- The difference is who decides, how long it takes, and what counts as proof —
  not the channels.
- B2B buyers manage risk and must justify the choice to someone else, so give
  them something forwardable.
- B2B decisions involve several people with different worries; produce something
  for each.
- B2C sells on personal appeal and works at reach; B2B works at depth on fewer
  accounts.
- B2B buyers are still people, and still ignore jargon.

lessons.title: Target audience and buyer personas
lessons.description: The four parts a persona needs, where to get them, and the test for whether it is useful.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Your **target audience** is the group of people you are trying to reach. A
**buyer persona** is a short, written description of one typical person from
that group, used to make decisions.

The audience is a category: *women aged 25 to 40 who care about ingredients*. The
persona is a person: *Priya, 32, works long hours, has sensitive skin, has
wasted money on products that broke her out, reads ingredient lists before she
buys.*

The persona is more useful because it answers questions the category cannot.
Should this email be long or short? Should we lead with price or with
ingredients? You cannot ask a category, but you can ask Priya.

### What a persona must contain

A persona is only worth writing if it changes a decision. Four parts earn their
place:

1. **The situation** — age range, job, and the circumstances that matter. Not a
   biography.
2. **The goal** — what they are actually trying to achieve. People do not want
   moisturiser; they want to stop worrying about their skin.
3. **The barriers** — what stops them buying. Cost, distrust, confusion, past
   disappointment, not knowing it exists.
4. **Where they already look** — the channels they use when they have this
   problem. This single line decides most of your channel strategy.

Anything else — favourite coffee, fictional surname, a stock photograph — is
decoration. It makes the document feel real without making it useful.

### An analogy

Writing for an audience is shouting into a crowded room. Writing for a persona
is talking to one person in that room. The odd thing is that the second one
reaches more people, because it sounds like it was meant for someone.

```
  TARGET AUDIENCE                      BUYER PERSONA
  +--------------------------+         +---------------------------+
  | women, 25-44             |         | Priya, 32, works late     |
  | urban                    |  ---->  | wants to stop worrying    |
  | interested in skincare   |         | about her skin            |
  | mid income               |         | burned before by products |
  +--------------------------+         | that broke her out        |
                                       | searches, reads reviews   |
  a group you can target               +---------------------------+
  in an ad platform                    a person you can write to

  You need both. The audience aims the ad. The persona writes it.
```

### Where personas come from

Not from imagination. The honest sources are: talking to customers, reading
reviews of competitors, reading the questions people ask in support, and search
data showing what people type. A persona invented in a meeting usually describes
the team, not the customer.

When you have no customers yet, write the persona from assumptions, **mark them
as assumptions**, and replace them as you learn. A guess you have labelled is
useful. A guess you have forgotten was a guess is dangerous.

## Demo

**Petal & Pine** writes two personas, because they found two genuinely different
buyers in their reviews.

**Persona 1 — Careful Priya, 32.**
*Situation:* works long hours, sensitive skin, buys online.
*Goal:* a routine that works and stops her thinking about it.
*Barriers:* has wasted money before; distrusts marketing claims; afraid of a
reaction.
*Where she looks:* searches symptoms, reads full ingredient lists, trusts
reviews from people with the same skin type.

What changes because of this: product pages lead with the full ingredient list
and reviews filtered by skin type, not with a discount. The checklist lead
magnet works because it is useful before she has spent anything.

**Persona 2 — Gifting Gina, 45.**
*Situation:* buying a present, not a user of the product.
*Goal:* something that looks thoughtful and will not go wrong.
*Barriers:* does not know the recipient's skin type; worried about picking the
wrong thing; buying close to a deadline.
*Where she looks:* searches gift guides, looks at photographs of packaging,
cares about delivery dates.

What changes because of this: a gift set with a safe, broadly suitable product,
clear delivery cut-offs, and a gift receipt. The ingredient list that convinces
Priya is irrelevant to Gina — she wants reassurance she cannot get it wrong.

Two personas, two different pages, one brand. Without the personas, Petal & Pine
would have written one page that half-served both.

## Hands-on practice

Write one persona for a business you know, using only evidence you can actually
point at. Where you are guessing, write GUESS next to it.

The GUESS labels are the most valuable thing on the sheet. They are your
research list.

:::worksheet Buyer persona sheet
Persona name and age:
Business they would buy from:

SITUATION
- Job or life stage:
- The circumstances that matter here:
- Source for this (review / conversation / search data / GUESS):

GOAL
- What are they actually trying to achieve?
- What would "solved" look like to them?
- Source:

BARRIERS
- What stops them buying?
- What have they been burned by before?
- What would they need to believe to go ahead?
- Source:

WHERE THEY ALREADY LOOK
- What do they type into a search engine?
- Which platforms, if any?
- Whose opinion do they trust?
- Source:

SO WHAT
- One thing this changes about the website:
- One thing this changes about the message:
- One channel this rules in or out:
:::

If the SO WHAT box is empty, the persona is decoration. Rewrite it.

## Common mistakes

**Inventing the persona in a meeting.** The result describes the team's
assumptions. Use reviews, support questions and search data instead — all three
are free.

**Adding detail that changes nothing.** A fictional surname and a stock photo
make it feel professional and help nobody. If a detail does not change a
decision, cut it.

**Writing one persona for everyone.** Petal & Pine's two buyers want opposite
things. Collapsing them produces a message that half-convinces both.

**Writing twelve personas.** Beyond three or four, nobody remembers them and
they stop being used. Two good ones beat ten filed ones.

**Never updating it.** A persona written at launch and untouched two years later
describes a customer who may no longer exist. Revisit it when the reviews start
saying something new.

## Key takeaways

- The audience aims the ad; the persona writes it. You need both.
- A persona needs four things: situation, goal, barriers, and where they already
  look.
- Build it from reviews, support questions and search data — not imagination.
- Label every guess, and treat the labels as your research list.
- If the persona does not change a decision, it is decoration.

lessons.title: Customer segmentation
lessons.description: Splitting an audience into groups you can actually select in a tool and message differently.
lessons.content:
## Learn

**Segmentation** is splitting your audience into groups that need different
marketing, then treating each group differently.

A persona describes a typical buyer. A segment is a group you can actually
*act* on — select in an email tool, target in an ad platform, or send down a
different path on your website. The test is simple: if you cannot separate the
group in a tool, it is not yet a segment.

### The four common ways to split

**Demographic** — age, gender, income, job title, company size. Easy to target,
often weakly related to what people actually want.

**Geographic** — country, city, distance from a shop. Essential for anything
local; a dental clinic's entire strategy is geographic.

**Behavioural** — what they have actually done: pages viewed, items bought, how
recently, how often, whether they opened the last five emails. Usually the most
predictive of the four.

**Psychographic** — attitudes and motivations: price-driven, ingredient-driven,
convenience-driven. The hardest to collect and often the most useful, because it
explains *why*.

Beginners reach for demographic because it is easiest. Behavioural is usually
the one that changes results, because what someone did last week predicts next
week better than their age does.

### An analogy

A shopkeeper who knows every customer does this instinctively. She greets the
regular differently from the stranger, mentions the new delivery to the person
who bought it last month, and does not try to sell nappies to the man who comes
in for a newspaper.

Segmentation is how you do that at a scale where you cannot know anyone
personally.

```
  ONE LIST                          SEGMENTED LIST
  +---------------------+           +---------------------------------+
  | 5,000 subscribers   |           | bought in last 60 days    (400) |
  | one email to all    |   --->    | bought once, long ago     (900) |
  |                     |           | never bought, opens often (1,800)|
  | "Our new serum!"    |           | never opened anything     (1,900)|
  +---------------------+           +---------------------------------+
                                       |        |        |         |
                                    reorder  win-back  first    clean
                                    prompt   offer     purchase  or drop
```

The four segments need four different messages. Sending the reorder prompt to
someone who has never bought is noise; sending the first-purchase offer to a
loyal customer gives away margin you did not need to give.

### How far to go

Segmentation has a cost: every segment is another message to write and maintain.
Split only where the message would genuinely differ. Three segments you actually
use beat twelve you do not.

A good rule: start by splitting on behaviour — bought or not, recent or not —
because those two lines alone usually explain most of the difference.

## Demo

**Petal & Pine** has an email list of five thousand. One message to everyone
performs poorly, so they split it four ways.

**Recent buyers (400).** Bought in the last sixty days. They do not need
convincing; they need to use the product properly and reorder on time. They get
usage tips and a reorder reminder timed to when the bottle runs low. No
discount — they have already paid full price.

**Lapsed buyers (900).** Bought once, more than six months ago. Something
stopped them. They get a short email asking what happened, and an offer to try
the newer formulation. This group responds best to being asked rather than sold
to.

**Engaged non-buyers (1,800).** On the list, open the emails, never purchased.
They are interested and unconvinced. They get reviews from people with similar
skin, and a smaller trial size to lower the risk of a first purchase.

**Dormant (1,900).** Have not opened anything in six months. They get one
re-permission email asking if they still want to hear from Petal & Pine. Those
who do not respond are removed — which sounds like losing 1,900 subscribers and
is actually protecting deliverability, covered in module 9.

**The result worth noticing.** The engaged non-buyers were the biggest
opportunity and were invisible on a single list. They had been getting reorder
reminders for a product they had never bought.

## Hands-on practice

Segment a list you can actually describe. Use your own inbox if you have no
business data: pick a brand that emails you and work out which segment you are
in and what they should be sending you.

:::worksheet Segmentation plan
Business:
Roughly how many people on the list:

SEGMENT 1
- Name:
- The rule that defines it (so a tool could select it):
- Roughly how many:
- What they need to hear:
- What they must NOT be sent:

SEGMENT 2
- Name:
- Rule:
- Roughly how many:
- What they need to hear:
- What they must NOT be sent:

SEGMENT 3
- Name:
- Rule:
- Roughly how many:
- What they need to hear:
- What they must NOT be sent:

CHECK
- Could a tool actually select each of these? If not, fix the rule.
- Which segment is the biggest missed opportunity?
- Which message am I currently sending to the wrong segment?
:::

## Common mistakes

**Splitting on demographics because it is easy.** Age rarely explains buying
behaviour as well as last purchase date does. Start with behaviour.

**Creating segments you cannot select.** "People who care about sustainability"
is a real group and not a segment until you have a way to identify them — a quiz
answer, a page they viewed, a product they bought.

**Over-segmenting.** Twelve segments means twelve messages to write every time.
Most teams quietly go back to sending one. Three used beats twelve ignored.

**Never removing anyone.** Keeping unengaged contacts to make the number look
big damages deliverability, so the people who do want your email stop receiving
it.

**Segmenting once and never revisiting.** Segments are states, not labels.
Today's recent buyer is next quarter's lapsed buyer, and the rules should move
them automatically.

## Key takeaways

- A segment is a group you can actually select in a tool and send something
  different to.
- The four bases are demographic, geographic, behavioural and psychographic;
  behavioural usually predicts best.
- Split only where the message would genuinely differ.
- Three segments you use beat twelve you file.
- Segments are states people move between, so the rules must update themselves.

lessons.title: Marketing objectives and KPIs
lessons.description: SMART objectives, leading and lagging indicators, and the test that exposes a vanity metric.
lessons.content:
## Learn

An **objective** is what you are trying to achieve. A **KPI**, or key
performance indicator, is the number that tells you whether you are achieving
it. A **metric** is any number you can measure; a KPI is one of the few you have
decided actually matters.

That last distinction matters more than it sounds. Analytics tools will show you
hundreds of metrics. Treating them all as important is the same as treating none
of them as important.

### Making an objective useful

"Grow the business" is a wish. A usable objective states what, how much, and by
when. The common shorthand is **SMART**: specific, measurable, achievable,
relevant and time-bound.

Compare:

- *Wish:* get more customers.
- *Objective:* increase online orders from 120 to 160 a month within one
  quarter.

The second one can be checked. It also tells you immediately whether your plan
is plausible — forty extra orders a month is a very different task from four.

### Leading and lagging indicators

**Lagging indicators** tell you what happened: revenue, orders, customers won.
They are what you actually care about, and they arrive too late to change.

**Leading indicators** move earlier and predict the lagging ones: enquiries,
email sign-ups, qualified traffic, trial starts. They are what you steer by
during the month.

A dashboard with only lagging indicators is a rear-view mirror. You need both.

```
  LEADING (steer by these)        LAGGING (judge by these)
  +------------------------+      +------------------------+
  | qualified visitors     |      | orders                 |
  | email sign-ups         | ---> | revenue                |
  | enquiries / trials     |      | new customers          |
  | add-to-cart rate       |      | repeat purchase rate   |
  +------------------------+      +------------------------+
     move this week                arrives next month
```

### Vanity metrics

A **vanity metric** is a number that reliably goes up and does not connect to
the objective. Follower counts, impressions and page views are the usual
suspects. They are not useless — impressions genuinely matter for awareness —
but they become vanity metrics when they are reported *instead of* the number
that matters.

The test: if this number doubled, would the business be better off? If you
cannot explain how, it is not a KPI.

### An analogy

Driving somewhere. The objective is arriving by six. Speed and fuel are leading
indicators you steer by. Arrival time is the lagging indicator. The number of
songs played is a metric that goes up reliably and tells you nothing.

## Demo

**Bright Mile Dental** sets objectives for one quarter.

**Business objective:** fill the three empty appointment slots each week.

**Marketing objective:** increase new-patient bookings from 18 a month to 30 a
month within one quarter.

**KPIs, in the order they move:**

| KPI | Type | Why it is here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clicks on *dentist near me* ads | Leading | First sign the campaign is reaching people |
| Booking-page visits | Leading | Shows the ad sent the right people |
| Booking form completions | Leading | The actual conversion step |
| New-patient bookings | Lagging | The objective itself |
| Cost per new patient | Lagging | Tells them whether it is worth continuing |

**What they deliberately do not track as a KPI:** social media followers. Bright
Mile has a page, and it is not how patients find a dentist. Following it would
feel like progress without producing any.

**What happened.** Clicks rose quickly, booking-page visits rose with them, and
form completions did not. The leading indicators isolated the problem in week
two: the ads worked and the booking form was broken on mobile. Without the
middle KPIs, they would have waited a month to discover bookings had not moved
and had no idea why.

That is the whole argument for leading indicators.

## Hands-on practice

Write one objective and its KPI set for a business you know. The hard part is
limiting yourself to five KPIs. If everything is a KPI, nothing is.

:::worksheet Objectives and KPIs
Business:

BUSINESS OBJECTIVE
- What the business needs (in plain words):

MARKETING OBJECTIVE (SMART)
- From ______ to ______ by ______
- Is this achievable with the resources available? If not, change the number.

KPIs (maximum five)
1. Name:          Leading or lagging:     Why it matters:
2. Name:          Leading or lagging:     Why it matters:
3. Name:          Leading or lagging:     Why it matters:
4. Name:          Leading or lagging:     Why it matters:
5. Name:          Leading or lagging:     Why it matters:

CHECKS
- Do I have at least two leading indicators I could act on this week?
- For each KPI: if it doubled, would the business be better off? How?
- Which number am I tempted to report that is really a vanity metric?
:::

## Common mistakes

**Setting objectives with no number or no date.** "Improve brand awareness" can
never be achieved or failed, which is precisely why it survives so long in
marketing plans.

**Tracking only lagging indicators.** You find out you missed the target after
it is too late to do anything, and with no clue where it went wrong.

**Reporting vanity metrics because they look good.** Impressions always rise if
you spend more. Rising impressions with flat enquiries is a problem being
reported as a success.

**Having fifteen KPIs.** Nobody acts on fifteen numbers. Five is a dashboard;
fifteen is a spreadsheet nobody opens.

**Setting a target with no basis.** "Triple our bookings" sounds ambitious and
usually means the plan was never checked against capacity, budget or the
conversion rates you already have.

## Key takeaways

- An objective says what, how much, and by when; anything vaguer cannot be
  checked.
- A KPI is one of the few metrics you have decided actually matters.
- Leading indicators let you steer this week; lagging indicators judge the
  quarter. You need both.
- A vanity metric is one that rises reliably without making the business better
  off.
- Cap the dashboard at about five KPIs so they get acted on.

lessons.title: How a digital marketing strategy fits together
lessons.description: The chain from objective to review that turns the previous eight lessons into one page.
lessons.content:
## Learn

A **digital marketing strategy** is a short set of decisions that explains who
you are selling to, what you want them to do, where you will reach them, and how
you will know whether it worked.

It is not a list of tactics. "Post three times a week, start a newsletter, run
some ads" is a to-do list. A strategy is the reasoning that makes a to-do list
obvious.

This lesson joins the previous eight together. Everything you have learned so
far is one input into the same document.

### The chain

Each link is decided by the one above it. That dependency is the whole idea.

```
  BUSINESS OBJECTIVE      what the business needs           (lesson 8)
          |
          v
  AUDIENCE AND PERSONA    who can give it to us             (lessons 6, 7)
          |
          v
  JOURNEY STAGE           what they need from us now        (lesson 4)
          |
          v
  CHANNELS                where they already are            (lesson 3)
          |
          v
  MESSAGE AND OFFER       what we say, and what we ask for
          |
          v
  KPIs                    how we will know                  (lesson 8)
          |
          v
  REVIEW                  what we change next month
```

Read it downwards and each choice is forced by the one above. Read it upwards
and you can justify every tactic. A tactic that cannot be traced back up this
chain should not be funded.

### Why strategies fail

Almost always because someone starts in the middle. A team decides it needs
short-form video, then works backwards to invent an audience that wants it. The
work gets done, the numbers do not move, and nobody can say why because there
was never a prediction to test.

### An analogy

A strategy is a route, not a destination and not a car. "Get to Manchester by
six" is the objective. "Drive" is a tactic. The strategy is: take the motorway
rather than the scenic road because we care about time, leave before four to
miss the traffic, and if the motorway is blocked we take this alternative.

The value is in the *because* and the *if*. Those are the parts a to-do list
leaves out.

### How long it should be

One page. A strategy nobody can hold in their head does not get followed. If it
runs to twenty pages, it is a plan document with a strategy hidden somewhere
inside it.

## Demo

**Craftwise Academy** writes its one-page strategy for the next quarter.

**Business objective.** Sell 200 seats on the new beginner course this quarter,
up from 120 last quarter.

**Audience and persona.** *Switching Sam, 26.* Works in a job he does not want to
stay in. Goal: a skill that leads to different work within a year. Barriers: has
started free courses before and abandoned them; unsure which course is
legitimate; nervous about wasting money. Looks: searches for comparisons and
reads reviews, watches a sample lesson before committing.

**Journey stage to focus on.** Consideration. Craftwise already gets visitors —
awareness is not the gap. People arrive, compare, and do not decide. So the work
goes into helping people choose, not into more traffic.

**Channels.** Search, because Sam searches comparisons. Email, because the
decision takes weeks and needs follow-up. Not short-form video this quarter:
Sam watches a sample lesson, not a thirty-second clip, and Craftwise cannot do
both well with the people it has.

**Message and offer.** The message is *know what you are signing up for before
you pay*. The offer is a genuinely free first module — not a trailer — plus an
honest comparison page that says who the course is **not** for.

**KPIs.**

| KPI | Type | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visits to the comparison page | Leading | 4,000 this quarter |
| Free first-module starts | Leading | 800 |
| Free-to-paid conversion rate | Leading | 25% |
| Seats sold | Lagging | 200 |
| Cost per seat sold | Lagging | Below last quarter's |

Those targets were worked backwards from the 200 seats: 4,000 visits, a fifth of
them starting the free module, a quarter of those paying. They are Craftwise's
own arithmetic, not industry benchmarks — your numbers will be different, and
anyone quoting you a standard conversion rate for your situation is guessing.

**Review.** Monthly. If free starts are high and conversion is low, the course
is not matching what the free module promised. If free starts are low, the
comparison page is not persuading. Each failure points at a different fix,
which is how you know the KPIs were chosen properly.

Notice what the strategy ruled *out*. Saying no to video is a strategic decision
and took one line. Most of the value in a strategy is in what it declines.

## Hands-on practice

Write a one-page strategy. Use a business you know well — your employer, a
family business, or one of the fictional brands from this course.

Keep it to one page. If it will not fit, you have written a plan, not a strategy.

:::template One-page digital marketing strategy
BUSINESS OBJECTIVE
What the business needs, with a number and a date:

AUDIENCE AND PERSONA
Who:
Their goal:
Their main barrier:
Where they already look:

JOURNEY STAGE
The stage where we are losing people:
How I know:

CHANNELS
Channel 1:                    because:
Channel 2:                    because:
Channel we are NOT using:     because:

MESSAGE AND OFFER
The one thing we want them to understand:
What we are asking them to do:
Why they would say yes:

KPIs (max five)
1.                            Leading / lagging       Target:
2.                            Leading / lagging       Target:
3.                            Leading / lagging       Target:
4.                            Leading / lagging       Target:
5.                            Leading / lagging       Target:

REVIEW
How often:
If the leading indicators are good but the lagging ones are not, we will:
If the leading indicators are bad, we will:
:::

## Common mistakes

**Starting with the channel.** "We need to be on TikTok" is a conclusion in
search of a reason. Start at the objective and let the channel fall out of it.

**Writing a strategy with nothing ruled out.** A document that approves every
channel has made no decisions. The no is the strategy.

**No journey stage.** Without naming where you are losing people, effort
defaults to getting more traffic, which is rarely the problem.

**Confusing the strategy with the plan.** The strategy is the reasoning; the
plan is the calendar. You need both, and only one of them is one page.

**Writing it once and never reviewing it.** A strategy with no review date is a
document. Monthly or quarterly review is what makes it a working tool.

## Key takeaways

- A strategy is the reasoning that makes the to-do list obvious, not the to-do
  list itself.
- The chain runs objective → audience → journey stage → channels → message →
  KPIs → review, and each link is forced by the one above.
- Any tactic that cannot be traced back up the chain should not be funded.
- Deciding what *not* to do is the most valuable part.
- Keep it to one page and give it a review date.

lessons.title: Practice questions: digital marketing fundamentals
lessons.description: Forty questions with answer keys: 20 multiple choice, 10 short answer, 5 scenarios, 5 true or false.
lessons.content:
## How to use this

Forty questions covering all nine lessons in this module: 20 multiple choice, 10
short answer, 5 scenarios and 5 true or false.

Answer before you check. Getting one wrong and understanding why is worth more
than getting it right by guessing. Nothing here is recorded.

## Multiple choice

:::quiz
Q. Which best describes digital marketing?
+ Finding, winning and keeping customers through digital channels
- Posting regularly on social media
- Buying advertising online
- Building a website
= It covers every digital channel and all three jobs: get found, get chosen, get kept. Posting and advertising are activities inside it, not the whole of it.

Q. A business gets plenty of website visitors but almost no sales. Which of the three jobs is failing?
- Get found
+ Get chosen
- Get kept
= The traffic proves "get found" is working. Visitors who arrive and do not act means the site is not convincing them.

Q. Why is it misleading to say digital marketing is free?
+ The time and skill needed to produce the work is a real cost
- Every digital channel charges per click
- Hosting a website is expensive
- Email tools always charge per subscriber
= Digital shifts the cost from buying media to time and skill. It does not remove the cost.

Q. What is the main targeting difference between traditional and digital marketing?
- Digital reaches more people
+ Traditional buys a location, digital buys an audience
- Traditional is always cheaper per person
- Digital works instantly and traditional does not
= A billboard is seen by whoever passes it. A search ad is seen by people who typed something specific.

Q. A clinic runs both a leaflet drop and search ads, but only measures the ads. What is the risk?
+ They will conclude ads work better simply because the leaflets were never measured
- The leaflets will make the ads more expensive
- The ads will stop being shown
- Nothing, because leaflets cannot be measured
= If you only count what is easy to count, you will always conclude the easy-to-count thing is better. Give the leaflet a trackable prompt first.

Q. Which of these is owned media?
- A page one search ranking
+ Your email list
- A sponsored post by a creator
- A mention in a news article
= Owned media is what you control and nobody can take away. Rankings and mentions are earned; sponsored posts are paid.

Q. Why is relying only on paid media risky?
+ The audience disappears the moment you stop paying
- Paid media cannot be measured
- Ad platforms do not allow long campaigns
- It only reaches people who already know you
= Paid media is rented attention. When the budget stops it leaves no asset behind.

Q. In the ecosystem, what do paid and earned media mainly exist to do?
+ Fill owned media
- Replace owned media
- Reduce the cost of running a website
- Improve the quality of your product
= Everything points at owned media, because that is the asset that remains.

Q. Someone has just discovered a brand for the first time. Which message fits best?
- A discount code expiring tonight
+ Something that genuinely helps with the problem they have
- A request to leave a review
- A reorder reminder
= At the awareness stage they are not ready to buy. Selling immediately usually loses them for good.

Q. Why does the advocacy stage feed back into the consideration stage?
+ Reviews and recommendations are what the next buyer compares
- Advocates spend more per order
- It automatically lowers advertising costs
- It shortens the sales cycle for everyone
= The funnel is a loop. Today's reviews become tomorrow's proof for someone still deciding.

Q. The funnel narrows at every stage. What does that mean?
+ It is normal, and the job is to narrow it less
- The targeting was wrong
- The marketing has failed
- The product is priced too high
= Numbers always shrink between stages. Improvement means improving the rate, not removing the narrowing.

Q. In B2B, why do case studies and references matter so much?
+ The buyer has to justify the decision to other people
- B2B buyers do not read advertising
- They are cheaper to produce than adverts
- Search engines rank them higher
= B2B buying is risk management. Proof is what makes a choice defensible to a colleague.

Q. A B2B campaign speaks only to the person who will use the product. What usually happens?
+ It stalls at the approval step
- It converts faster than usual
- It reaches a wider audience
- It lowers the cost per lead
= The user often cannot sign anything. The budget holder has different worries and needs their own material.

Q. Which statement is true of both B2B and B2C marketing?
+ The reader is a person who ignores jargon
- The decision is made by one person
- The sales cycle is measured in minutes
- Emotional appeal plays no part
= B2B buyers are still human. Grey, formal content performs worse in both.

Q. What makes a buyer persona useful rather than decorative?
+ It changes a decision you would otherwise have made differently
- It includes a name, age and photograph
- It covers every type of customer you have
- It is approved by the whole team
= If a detail changes nothing, cut it. The "so what" box is the test.

Q. Where should the content of a buyer persona come from?
+ Reviews, support questions, customer conversations and search data
- A brainstorm with the marketing team
- The competitor's about page
- Industry reports about the sector
= A persona invented in a meeting usually describes the team rather than the customer.

Q. What makes a group an actual segment rather than just a description?
+ You can select it in a tool and send it something different
- It shares an age range
- It contains more than one hundred people
- It has been approved by management
= If you cannot separate the group in an email or ad tool, it is a description you cannot act on.

Q. Which basis for segmentation usually predicts buying behaviour best?
+ Behavioural
- Demographic
- Geographic
- Alphabetical
= What someone actually did recently predicts next week far better than their age does.

Q. What is a leading indicator?
+ A number that moves early and predicts a later result
- The most important number on the dashboard
- Any number reported to senior management
- A number that only goes up
= Leading indicators let you steer during the month. Lagging indicators judge it afterwards.

Q. Which of these is a strategy rather than a tactic?
+ We will focus on consideration, because visitors arrive and then fail to decide
- We will post three times a week
- We will start a newsletter
- We will redesign the home page
= A strategy carries the reasoning. The others are to-do items with no "because" attached.
:::

## Short answer

Write your answer down before opening each solution. Writing it out is the part
that tests whether you actually know it.

**1. In one sentence, what are the three jobs every piece of digital marketing does?**

:::solution
Get found, get chosen, and get kept — bringing a stranger to you, convincing
them to act, and bringing them back.
:::

**2. Give one reason a leaflet drop might beat a search ad for a brand-new clinic.**

:::solution
Nobody searches for a name they have never heard. Search ads catch people
already looking, but a brand-new clinic has no awareness at all, and a leaflet
creates it across the local area in a way search cannot.
:::

**3. Name the three media types and give one example of each.**

:::solution
Owned (your email list, your website), earned (a search ranking, a review, a
recommendation) and paid (search ads, social ads, sponsorships).
:::

**4. Why is it a mistake to stop the funnel at conversion?**

:::solution
Retention and advocacy are where repeat profit and social proof come from.
Winning back an existing customer is usually far easier than finding a new one,
because trust already exists, and advocacy produces the reviews that convince
the next buyer.
:::

**5. Name two people other than the user who may be involved in a B2B decision, and say what each worries about.**

:::solution
The budget holder, who worries about cost and whether the spend is justifiable;
and an IT or security contact, who worries about where data is stored and
whether it creates risk. Procurement and legal are also common.
:::

**6. What four parts must a buyer persona contain?**

:::solution
The situation, the goal, the barriers, and where they already look. Anything
else is decoration unless it changes a decision.
:::

**7. Give an example of a group that is not yet a segment, and say what would turn it into one.**

:::solution
"People who care about sustainability" is a real group but not a segment,
because there is no way to select them. It becomes a segment once you can
identify them — for example by a quiz answer, a page they viewed, or a product
they bought.
:::

**8. Explain the difference between a metric and a KPI.**

:::solution
A metric is any number you can measure. A KPI is one of the small number of
metrics you have decided actually matters for this objective. Analytics tools
show hundreds of metrics; treating them all as important is the same as
treating none of them as important.
:::

**9. Give one vanity metric and explain the test that exposes it.**

:::solution
Follower count is the usual example. The test: if this number doubled, would the
business be better off, and can I explain how? If not, it is a vanity metric.
Note that a metric is not vanity in itself — impressions genuinely matter for
awareness — it becomes one when reported instead of the number that matters.
:::

**10. Your team says "we need a YouTube channel". What do you ask first, and why?**

:::solution
Ask what the business objective is and where the audience already looks. The
channel should fall out of those two answers. Starting with the channel means
working backwards to invent a reason, and if it fails nobody can say why,
because there was never a prediction to test.
:::

## Scenario questions

:::quiz
Q. Petal & Pine discovers that 1,800 people on its email list open every message
but have never bought anything, and they have been receiving reorder reminders
for a product they do not own. What is the best next step?
+ Send that group reviews from similar customers and a smaller trial size
- Remove them from the list, since they clearly will not buy
- Send them the reorder reminder more often
- Offer the whole list a discount
= They are interested and unconvinced, which is a consideration problem. Lowering the risk of a first purchase addresses it. The reorder reminder was simply the wrong message for the segment.

Q. Bright Mile Dental's search ad clicks rise sharply, booking-page visits rise
with them, but booking form completions stay flat. What does this most likely
indicate?
+ Something on the booking page or form is broken or confusing
- The ads are targeting the wrong people
- The clinic's prices are too high
- The campaign needs a bigger budget
= The leading indicators isolate the problem. People are arriving at the right page, so targeting is fine; they are failing at the final step, which points at the form.

Q. A Shiftly sales conversation goes well, the operations manager is
enthusiastic, and then nothing happens for three weeks. What is most likely
missing?
+ Material the manager can forward to the budget holder and IT
- A discount to create urgency
- More frequent follow-up calls
- A better product demonstration
= The user is convinced but cannot sign. B2B stalls at approval when nobody has given the enthusiastic person something defensible to pass on.

Q. Craftwise Academy sees high numbers starting its free first module but very
few converting to the paid course. What does this most likely tell them?
+ The paid course is not matching what the free module led people to expect
- The comparison page is not persuading people
- They should stop offering the free module
- They need more traffic
= High starts mean the top of the journey works. The drop is at the point where the promise meets the product, so the mismatch is there.

Q. A small business reaches its entire audience through one social media account
and wants to reduce its risk. What should it do first?
+ Start converting followers into an email list it owns
- Open accounts on three more social platforms
- Increase how often it posts
- Buy ads to grow the following faster
= The risk is building on rented land. More rented land is still rented. Owned media is the only thing that cannot be taken away by a policy change.
:::

## True or false

:::quiz
Q. True or false: digital marketing always costs less per customer won than traditional marketing.
- True
+ False
= Competitive search terms can cost more per enquiry than a leaflet drop. Cheaper per person reached is not the same as cheaper per customer won.

Q. True or false: owned media is the asset that remains when advertising spend stops.
+ True
- False
= That is exactly why paid and earned media exist to fill it. Paid attention disappears with the budget; an email list does not.

Q. True or false: when a business has no customers yet, a persona should simply be imagined.
- True
+ False
= It should be built from assumptions that are clearly labelled as assumptions, then replaced as you learn. A labelled guess is useful; a forgotten guess is dangerous.

Q. True or false: impressions are always a vanity metric.
- True
+ False
= Impressions genuinely matter for an awareness objective. A metric becomes a vanity metric when it is reported instead of the number that matters, not because of what it measures.

Q. True or false: every tactic in a marketing plan should trace back to the business objective.
+ True
- False
= That chain is what separates a strategy from a to-do list. A tactic that cannot be traced back up it should not be funded.
:::

## Where to look if you got one wrong

- Questions about the three jobs or what digital marketing is — lesson 1
- Traditional versus digital, and measuring both fairly — lesson 2
- Owned, earned and paid media — lesson 3
- Funnel stages and the loop back to consideration — lesson 4
- B2B decision makers and proof — lesson 5
- What belongs in a persona and where it comes from — lesson 6
- What makes a group a segment — lesson 7
- Objectives, KPIs, leading indicators and vanity metrics — lesson 8
- Strategy versus tactics, and the chain — lesson 9

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: a buyer persona and funnel for Petal & Pine
lessons.description: Three guided exercises with expected output: build a persona from reviews, map the funnel, choose KPIs.
lessons.content:
## What you will build

Three connected pieces of work for **Petal & Pine**, the fictional D2C skincare
brand: a buyer persona built from evidence, a funnel map that finds the gap, and
a KPI set that would catch the problem early.

This is the practical listed for this module in the course outline. Allow about
an hour. Everything you need is on this page — no accounts, no tools beyond
something to write in.

This module has no coding exercises. Code appears in modules 2, 3, 11, 15 and
17, where a marketer genuinely needs it.

## Before you start

Copy the template at the bottom of this page into a document. Work in it as you
go, because exercise 2 uses your answer from exercise 1, and exercise 3 uses
your answer from exercise 2.

---

## Exercise 1: build a persona from evidence

Below are six review snippets left on Petal & Pine's product pages. They are
fictional, written for this exercise.

```
R1  "Took a chance after my last moisturiser gave me a rash. Checked the
     ingredient list twice before ordering. Three weeks in, no reaction."
                                               - verified buyer, sensitive skin

R2  "Bought as a birthday present for my sister. The box looked lovely.
     I have no idea if it suits her skin but she seemed happy."
                                               - verified buyer

R3  "I don't have time to think about skincare. Two steps, morning and
     night, done. That's why I stuck with it."
                                               - verified buyer

R4  "Wanted something for my mum for Christmas and panicked about delivery.
     The cut-off date was clearly stated which is why I ordered here."
                                               - verified buyer

R5  "Spent years buying things that broke me out. I now read every label.
     This one is honest about what's in it, which is rare."
                                               - verified buyer, sensitive skin

R6  "Fine product. I only bought it because my sister recommended it, I
     wouldn't have found it otherwise."
                                               - verified buyer
```

**Your task.** Two distinct buyers are visible in these six reviews. Identify
them, then write the one that is buying *for themselves* as a full persona:
situation, goal, barriers, where they look, and a "so what" line.

**Expected output.** Yours will be worded differently. It should contain the
same substance:

```
PERSONA: Careful Priya, early 30s
Evidence: R1, R3, R5

SITUATION  Busy, limited time for a routine. Sensitive skin. Buys online.
GOAL       A simple routine that works, so she can stop thinking about it.
BARRIERS   Has had a bad reaction before (R1). Has wasted money on products
           that broke her out (R5). Distrusts marketing claims.
LOOKS      Reads full ingredient lists before ordering (R1, R5). Trusts
           reviews from people with the same skin type.

SO WHAT
- Website: lead the product page with the full ingredient list, not a discount
- Message: be honest about what is in it, including who it is not for
- Channel: search, because she researches before buying

SECOND BUYER SPOTTED: the gift buyer (R2, R4) - wants reassurance they cannot
pick wrong, and a clear delivery cut-off. Different person, different page.
```

**Check yourself.** If your persona has a surname, a favourite drink or a photo
and no "so what" line, you have written decoration. R6 is a deliberate
distractor: it tells you about a channel (word of mouth), not about a person.

---

## Exercise 2: map the funnel and find the gap

Petal & Pine currently has these six marketing assets:

```
A  A blog article: "Why does my skin get dry in winter?"
B  A product page with photographs and the full ingredient list
C  A free winter skincare checklist, given in exchange for an email address
D  A reorder reminder email, sent six weeks after purchase
E  A paid social ad showing the product with the line "Shop now"
F  An email asking for a review, sent two weeks after the second order
```

**Your task.** Place each asset at the funnel stage it serves: awareness,
interest, consideration, conversion, retention, advocacy. Then name the stage
with no asset at all, and say what you would build for it.

**Expected output.**

```
AWARENESS       A (article), E (paid social ad)
INTEREST        C (checklist for an email address)
CONSIDERATION   -- nothing --
CONVERSION      B (product page)
RETENTION       D (reorder reminder)
ADVOCACY        F (review request)

THE GAP: consideration.

Someone has given their email address and is now comparing Petal & Pine with
alternatives, and nothing helps them decide. They go from "I am interested" to
a product page that assumes they have already chosen.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD
An honest comparison email: which moisturiser type suits which skin, including
when you do not need theirs. It earns trust at exactly the moment the buyer is
suspicious of being sold to.
```

**Check yourself.** Asset E is worth arguing about. "Shop now" sounds like
conversion, but a cold paid social ad reaches people who have never heard of the
brand, so it is doing an awareness job with a conversion message — which is the
mismatch lesson 4 warned about. Either answer is defensible if you explain it.

---

## Exercise 3: choose KPIs that would have caught it

Here are ten things Petal & Pine could measure.

```
1  Instagram followers              6  Email list size
2  Blog visitors from search        7  Reorder rate
3  Checklist sign-ups               8  Total page views
4  Product page visits              9  Reviews received
5  Orders                          10  Cost per order
```

**Your task.** Choose a maximum of five as KPIs for the objective *increase
first-time orders this quarter*. Label each leading or lagging. Then explain
which one would have revealed the consideration gap from exercise 2.

**Expected output.**

```
OBJECTIVE  Increase first-time orders this quarter

KPI                          TYPE       WHY
3  Checklist sign-ups        Leading    Interest stage is working
4  Product page visits       Leading    People are moving towards buying
5  Orders                    Lagging    The objective itself
10 Cost per order            Lagging    Tells us whether it is worth repeating
7  Reorder rate              Lagging    Guards against buying bad first orders

WHICH ONE REVEALS THE GAP
Checklist sign-ups rising while product page visits stay flat. People are
becoming leads and then not progressing - which is exactly the missing
consideration stage.

RULED OUT
1  Instagram followers - would rise without helping; vanity for this objective
8  Total page views    - too vague to act on
```
